theory.intro: A **scatter plot** shows bivariate data on the Cartesian plane. Each individual gives one point $(x, y)$, where $x$ is its independent-variable value and $y$ its dependent-variable value. The pattern the points form shows the relationship.
facts: Each individual contributes exactly **one point** $(x, y)$: $x$ is its horizontal-axis value and $y$ its vertical-axis value.
Choose an axis scale that fits the full range of the data, starting near the data rather than always at $0$.
A scale that starts near the data keeps the points spread out and readable.
**Label both axes** with the variable name and its units.
steps: Choose a scale for each axis that covers the full range of that variable's values.
Label both axes with the variable name and units.
Plot each data pair as a point at $(x, y)$.
Check that the number of points plotted equals the number of individuals in the data.

foundation.question_text:
A table gives students' heights ranging from $148$ cm to $186$ cm.
Which axis scale would let all the data fit comfortably on the plot: starting at $0$ cm in steps of $50$ cm, or starting at $145$ cm in steps of $5$ cm?
foundation.solution_text:
Starting at $0$ cm in steps of $50$ cm would squeeze every height between $148$ and $186$ cm into less than one grid square — the points would be almost impossible to tell apart.
Starting at $145$ cm in steps of $5$ cm spreads the same range of heights across about $8$ grid squares, so individual points can be read clearly.
Start at $145$ cm in steps of $5$ cm.

development.question_text:
Neither height nor arm span clearly causes the other, but a scatter plot still needs one variable on each axis.
Height is quick to measure with a tape measure; arm span is the value being estimated from it.
Which variable would most sensibly be plotted on the horizontal axis?
Explain your choice.
development.solution_text:
The variable that is already known, and used to estimate the other, is conventionally placed on the horizontal axis.
Height is measured first and used to estimate arm span, so height plays the role of the "known" variable here.
Height belongs on the horizontal axis; arm span belongs on the vertical axis.

mastery.question_text:
The table shows the height and arm span of $8$ students.
$\begin{array}{c|cccccccc} \text{Student} & \text{Amir} & \text{Bea} & \text{Cody} & \text{Dina} & \text{Ezra} & \text{Farah} & \text{Gia} & \text{Hugo} \\ \hline \text{Height (cm)} & 150 & 155 & 160 & 165 & 170 & 175 & 180 & 185 \\ \text{Arm span (cm)} & 145 & 160 & 155 & 170 & 165 & 180 & 175 & 190 \end{array}$
Choose a suitable scale for each axis, label both axes, and plot the data as a scatter plot.
